opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's one of the hardest questions, because writing is so subjective, and I think a lot of people underestimate how much taste goes into it. For me, it starts with a few things that sound simple but are surprisingly hard for models.

First, does it actually say something? A lot of model writing is fluent but empty. It hedges everything, it summarizes instead of committing to a point of view, and you finish reading it and nothing has changed in your head. Good writing has specificity. It picks the concrete detail over the generic one. If a model writes "the city was bustling," that's fine, but a good writer would tell you about the guy yelling at the pigeons outside the bodega. Specificity is a pretty strong signal.

Second, is it surprising in a way that still feels inevitable? That's what I love in fiction and poetry. The best line is one you didn't predict, but once you read it you feel like it couldn't have been anything else. Models are trained to predict the likely next token, so they naturally drift toward the average, the cliché. Pushing against that without becoming random or purple is a real craft problem.

Third, voice and audience awareness. Does the writing sound like someone in particular? Does it know who it's talking to? A great email to your manager and a great short story need totally different things, so "good" depends on the task. That's why I don't think you can have one universal writing metric. You need evals that are grounded in the context and the intent of the user.

And then practically, how do you measure it? I think you need a mix. You need people with real taste, writers, editors, people who read a lot, doing side-by-side comparisons and explaining why they prefer one output. The explanations matter more than the preference, because that's where you learn what the model's failure modes are. Things like overusing certain words, always ending with a neat moral, being too sycophantic, the same rhythm in every paragraph. Once you can name those patterns, you can build more targeted evals and even use models as graders for some of them, though I'd be careful there, because models grading models tends to reward the same blandness you're trying to get rid of.

So for me, good writing is: specific, has a point of view, surprises you, fits its audience, and respects the reader's intelligence. And the eval question is really how you encode taste without flattening it.

r001.rationale: It says writing quality depends on the task and calls for evaluations grounded in context and user intent, with different standards for an email and a short story.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's one of the hardest questions, because the moment you try to pin "good writing" down into a rubric, you start optimizing for the rubric and not for the writing. Like, if I say good writing is clear and concise, the model learns to be clear and concise in a way that's kind of dead. Every sentence is fine and the whole thing has no pulse.

So the way I think about it is less "what are the properties of good text" and more "what does a really good editor notice." An editor doesn't read with a checklist. They read and they feel friction. They notice where they got bored, where they had to reread something, where the writer was hedging because they didn't actually know what they thought. And a lot of evaluating model writing is trying to recover that sensibility.

A few things I actually look for. One is whether the model has a point of view. Not opinions for the sake of it, but does the piece know what it's about? A lot of model writing is a tour of everything related to the topic rather than an argument. Two is specificity. Weak writing lives in abstractions, "various factors," "a range of considerations." Good writing commits to a concrete example and lets it do the work. Three is rhythm, honestly. Sentence length variation, knowing when to stop. Models love symmetry, three bullet points, parallel structure, a little summary at the end. Humans don't write like that unless they're writing a memo.

And then there's the register problem, which I think is underrated. Good writing is good for a reader in a context. A text to a friend, a technical doc, an essay: they have completely different standards. So a lot of what I'm evaluating is whether the model read the room. Did it match the user's tone, the user's level of expertise, the amount of effort the moment called for? A beautifully composed five-paragraph response to a yes-or-no question is bad writing.

The honest answer on the methodology side is that I rely a lot on taste, mine and other people's, and then I try to make that taste legible. You collect pairs where you strongly prefer one response and you ask yourself why, and you write that down, and over time you get something like a style guide that's grounded in actual judgments rather than principles you made up in advance. It's slow. But I'd rather have a small amount of high-quality, high-agreement signal than a huge amount of "rate this one to seven" data where nobody really knows what a five means.

r001.rationale: The response discusses criteria for good writing and context-specific standards, but it frames rubrics as something that can distort evaluation and does not clearly state that evaluation uses rubrics defining what makes each type of writing good.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: good writing for whom, and for what purpose? A good answer to a technical question is very different from a good short story. So I’d start with the intent and the audience, rather than treating writing quality as one universal score.

Then I’d look at things like clarity, structure, specificity, and whether the response actually says something. Models can produce prose that sounds polished but doesn’t give you much information. If you strip away the formatting and the confident tone, is there still a useful idea there?

There’s also a subjective component. Two people can prefer different voices, and both preferences can be reasonable. In an evaluation, I’d want to distinguish those preferences from more concrete failures, like repetition, contradictions, or missing the point of the request. The goal is to understand what makes one response work better in that particular context.

r001.rationale: The response says writing quality depends on purpose and audience and names evaluation dimensions, but it does not state that evaluation uses rubrics defining what makes each type of writing good.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is, good writing for whom, and for what purpose? A clear technical explanation and a compelling short story need very different things. So I’d start with the reader’s intent: did the model actually communicate what they needed, in a voice that fits the situation?

Then I’d look at things like clarity, specificity, structure, and whether the writing earns its length. A response can be grammatically polished and still say very little. That’s why I wouldn’t want to reduce writing quality to a single score. Comparing examples and articulating why one works better can be much more useful than simply labeling something “good.”

r001.rationale: The candidate names general qualities such as clarity, specificity, and structure, and says standards depend on purpose. It does not state that evaluation uses rubrics defining what makes the particular type of writing good.
